Thioglycollate-induced peritonitis For the induction of sterile peritonitis, mice were intraperitoneally injected with a single dose of 2% sterile thioglycolate solution (in 0.3M NaHCO3, volume of 200uL; stock solution was allowed to age for three weeks at room temperature in the dark before injection) and sacrificed 72 hrs post injection for isolation and characterization of thioglycolate-elicited peritoneal macrophages. Cytokine and chemokine measurements Secreted human IL-1β and IL-10 were measured using the Human IL-1β/IL-1F2 DuoSet Kit or the Human IL-10 Quantikine Elisa kit (R&D Systems, DY201 and D1000B, respectively). Additional cytokines, growth factors and proteins (TNF, G-CSF, IL-6, IL-5, FGF, Arginase, IL-1RA, etc.) were quantified using a custom-assembled Human Multiplex Cytokine Assay (Bio-Plex; Bio-Rad Laboratories Inc.). Mouse IL-1β measured by either utilizing the Mouse IL-1 beta/IL-1F2 DuoSet ELISA kit (R&D Systems, DY401; recognizes predominantly mature IL-1β), via intracellular staining, or with the LEGENDplex ™ Mouse Inflammation Panel (13-plex) (BioLegend, 140150). The latter kit was also used to assess the additional mouse cytokines measured in this study. Activation of purified mitochondria The crude mitochondrial (Mc) fraction was further assessed for responsiveness towards C5a activation. Purified Mc were resuspended in mitochondria resuspension buffer prepared according to Wieckowski et al .( ). The solution containing Mc was distributed into equal volumes and treated with buffer or with increasing amounts of serum purified C5a (5–100 ng/ml, CompTech) at 30 °C with and without inhibitors for indicated time points. Mitochondria were then pelleted at 7000 × g , washed, and utilized in subsequent desired assays. Confocal microscopy of isolated mitochondria Mitochondrial fractions were fixed and permeabilized using the Fixation/Permeabilization kit (BD Biosciences) and stained with the indicated primary antibodies: anti-C5aR1 (1 μg/ml) and anti-TOM20 (1 μg/ml) overnight. After blocking with 20 % human serum, Mc were stained for 1 hr, at 4 °C, with highly cross-absorbed secondary antibodies (Invitrogen), at a concentration of 1 μg/mL: goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 488 (A11034) and goat anti-rabbit Atto 647N (Sigma Aldrich). Mc were mounted on coverslips using ProLong Diamond antifade mountant (Invitrogen, P36970 ), and images acquired using a Leica SP8 STED 3x microscope (Leica Microsystems) with usage of Huyguens and ImageJ softwares for image processing. Images were acquired as Z-stacks, through a 63x/1.4 oil-immersion objective, using 488 nm, 633 nm white laser lines for detection. Z-stacks images were deconvolved using SVI Huygens before generating single micrographs, with Fiji (version 2.1.0/1.52t) and JaCoP plugin used for detecting C5aR1 and TOM20 colocalization. Cell death assays During FACS-based measurements, viability of cells was routinely monitored by cell staining with an appropriate LIVE/DEAD Fixable Near-IR stain (Thermofisher Scientific). Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) assay . Monocytes or macrophages were cultured as indicated in the experiments. Cell death/cytotoxicity, as determined by LDH release, was assayed in culture supernatants using a calorimetric LDH Assay Kit (CyQUANT ™ LDH Cytotoxicity Assay; Invitrogen, C20301 ). ATP production . Cell death was also measured using the CellTiter-Glo® 3D Cell Viability Assay (Promega, G9681), which assesses overall ATP production by cells as a measure of viability. Cytochrome c release measurements To assess cytoplasmic cytochrome c in human and mouse monocytes or macrophages, the Human Cytochrome c Quantikine ELISA kit (DCTC0) or the Rat/Mouse Cytochrome c Quantikine ELISA kit (MCTC0, both from R&D Systems), respectively, were used according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Glucose uptake measurement Glucose uptake capacity by resting and crystal-sensing human monocytes was measured by uptake of the fluorescent 2-deoxy-D-glucose analog 2-[N-(7-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazol-4-yl)amino]-2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-NBDG; Sigma Aldrich, 72987). Briefly, human monocytes were resuspended in 250 μl RPMI/10 % FCS containing 20 μM 2-NBDG. Cells were either left non-activated, primed with LPS for 2 hrs and then exposed to cholesterol crystals for an additional 2 hrs at 37 °C and 5 % CO 2 prior to washing twice with FACS buffer. 2-NBDG uptake was then assessed by flowcytometry on a FACSCanto II ™ (BD Biosciences) and data analyzed using FlowJo (FlowJo, LLC). ADP, ATP, and cyclic AMP production by mitochondria Time-course measurement of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) generation was performed on purified mitochondria treated with purified C5a (10

72987). Briefly, human monocytes were resuspended in 250 μl RPMI/10 % FCS containing 20 μM 2-NBDG. Cells were either left non-activated, primed with LPS for 2 hrs and then exposed to cholesterol crystals for an additional 2 hrs at 37 °C and 5 % CO 2 prior to washing twice with FACS buffer. 2-NBDG uptake was then assessed by flowcytometry on a FACSCanto II ™ (BD Biosciences) and data analyzed using FlowJo (FlowJo, LLC). ADP, ATP, and cyclic AMP production by mitochondria Time-course measurement of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) generation was performed on purified mitochondria treated with purified C5a (10 or 20 ng/ml) for indicated time points. The Direct cAMP ELISA Kit (Enzo Life Science, ADI-900–066) was used for measurements according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For assessment of the ADP/ATP ratio of mitochondria, the ADP/ATP Quantification Bioluminescent Kit (Sigma Aldrich, MAK135) was used, according to the manufacturés protocol. Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) quantification Purified mitochondria . Isolated crude mitochondria were incubated with 1 μM of CM-H 2 TMROS or 5 μM of MitoSOX (Thermofisher Scientific) reagent at 30 °C, for 30 minutes, prior to treatment with PMX53 (10 μM) and activation with C5a (see above). The CM-H 2 TMROS or MitoSOX fluorescence was then measured using λex/em= 554⁄576 nm. The fluorescence intensity measured from mitochondria without CM-H 2 TMROS or MitoSOX treatment served as basal background signal and was subtracted before analysis. Whole cells . Cells were harvested, washed twice in 1 × PBS, and mitochondrial ROS production assessed by flowcytometry. ROS production in mouse BMDM or thioglycolate-elicited macrophages was measured in a similar fashion after appropriate stimulation. Mitochondrial mass assessment Human purified monocytes were pre-incubated with either PMX53 or JPE1375 (10 μM) or carrier solution and left non-activated or were primed with LPS (500 pg/ml, 2 hrs) and/or CC (500 mg/ml, 4 hrs). The media was then removed and replaced with pre-warmed media without FCS containing 10 nM of MitoTracker ™ Green FM and 50 nM of MitoTracker ™ Red FM (Thermofisher Scientific) for 30 min. Cells were washed twice with 1 × PBS and mitochondrial mass (MitoTracker Green) and membrane potential (MitoTracker Red) assessed by flowcytometry. Changes in mitochondrial mass were as via (MFI, MitoTracker Green) / (MFI, MitoTracker Red). Statistical analyses Analyses were performed with GraphPad Prism. Data are presented as mean ± SEM and analyzed using either Wilcoxon matched-paired signed rank test, or one-way ANOVA or wo-way ANOVA, with Bonferroni’s multiple comparison test, as appropriate. P values < 0.05 denote statistical significance. All experiments were carried out in duplicate technical and biological replicate unless otherwise stated. documents.title: Anesthesia and analgesia for hip fracture in older adults consensus statement

chunks.content: Introduction Hip fractures represent a major public health issue and are the most severe yet common consequence of osteoporosis [ – ]. They account for a substantial loss of healthy life years, driven by high rates of complications, mortality, long-term disability, and loss of autonomy [ , , – ]. The rising incidence of hip fractures due to demographic aging is already imposing significant costs on healthcare systems worldwide [ , ]. Effective management of hip fractures is therefore a priority to reduce their burden on individuals, society and healthcare infrastructures. While many risk factors are well known, yet largely non-modifiable [ , ], timing of surgical intervention is a critical modifiable factor influencing patient outcomes. Timely surgery is essential to alleviate pain, enable early mobilization, and prevent complications, such as urinary tract infections (OR 0.57 [ ], 0.44 [ ]), pneumonia (OR 0.83 [ ]), congestive heart failure (OR 0.77 [ ]), delirium (0.47 [ , ]), pressure ulcers (OR 0.55 [ ]; 0.25 [ ]), deep vein thrombosis (OR 0.61 [ ]; OR 1.1/d [ ]). Furthermore, prolonged bedrest leads to muscular and systemic deconditioning [ ]. Conversely, delayed surgery is associated with longer hospital stays, higher complication rates, and increased mortality [ , , – ]. Current international guidelines recommend surgery within 24 to 48 h of hospital admission, with some advocating for even earlier intervention [ , – ]. However, the precise threshold for acceptable delay remains under debate, complicated by conflicting study results and logistical feasibility [ , , , , , , – ]. Importantly, evidence on the timing of surgery often overlooks distinctions between different hip fracture types - particularly trochanteric versus femoral neck fractures. These subtypes vary in anatomical location, treatment strategies, patient demographics, and clinical outcomes. Trochanteric fractures - being extracapsular – are associated with a higher primary blood loss than intracapsular femoral neck fractures [ ]. They are usually managed with closed reduction and intramedullary nailing, a procedure that is relatively fast, resource-efficient, and technically less demanding than arthroplasty [ , ]. In contrast, femoral neck fractures are intracapsular and commonly require internal fixation or hip arthroplasty. Patients with trochanteric fractures tend to be older, with lower baseline mobility and fitness, and have worse clinical outcomes including higher complication and mortality rates, as well as prolonged hospitalization and rehabilitation [ , – ]. Grouping both fracture types in research may obscure important fracture-specific insights – highlighting the need for more targeted research on the optimal timing of surgery, particularly for trochanteric fractures. A further complication lies in the challenge of performing hip fracture surgery during nighttime hours. Despite the urgency of timely intervention, overnight procedures raise safety concerns due to surgeon fatigue, reduced staffing, and slower workflows [ ]. These system-level barriers can undermine guideline adherence and make scheduling within the recommended timeframe difficult. Balancing the benefits of early surgery with the potential risks of nighttime operations remains a pressing issue, particularly as healthcare systems strive to optimize outcomes under constrained resources. Aim This study investigates the influence of preoperative delay and nighttime surgery on in-hospital complication and mortality rates in patients with trochanteric fractures. We hypothesize that surgery performed within 24 h improves outcomes, irrespective of whether it is performed during day- or nighttime. With the fracture-specific focus of this research, we seek to address the limitations of prior studies and contribute evidence regarding the optimal timing of surgery for trochanteric hip fractures. Our findings aim to guide clinical practice and improve outcome. Materials and methods Study design and setting We analyzed the data of patients with trochanteric femur fractures from the prospective surgical registry of the working group for quality assurance in surgery (“Arbeitsgemeinschaft für Qualitätssicherung in der Chirurgie” or AQC). The AQC is a voluntary association of physicians in Switzerland formed with the aim of evaluating the in-hospital outcomes of surgical patients. Since almost 30 years 166 departments/attending doctors contributed 2.1 million anonymized cases with the purpose of ensuring surgical quality in Switzerland [ ]. The database contains information about (a) the hospitalization and (b) the procedure(s). The diagnosis is coded according to the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Edition (ICD-10) - a clinical cataloguing system developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) [ ]. Procedures are coded according to the Swiss operation classification ‘CHOP’ [ ]. Because only de-identified data from this national database was used, no institutional review board approval was required. Study subjects The inclusion criteria for the current study consisted of patients with the main diagnosis trochanteric femur fractures (ICD code S72.1) and main surgery by closed reduction and internal fixation (CRIF, CHOP code 79.15). Under the considerations of ICD and CHOP 9094 patients were elicited, 1910 cases were excluded due to missing data, especially the starting time of the surgery to ensure

by the World Health Organization (WHO) [ ]. Procedures are coded according to the Swiss operation classification ‘CHOP’ [ ]. Because only de-identified data from this national database was used, no institutional review board approval was required. Study subjects The inclusion criteria for the current study consisted of patients with the main diagnosis trochanteric femur fractures (ICD code S72.1) and main surgery by closed reduction and internal fixation (CRIF, CHOP code 79.15). Under the considerations of ICD and CHOP 9094 patients were elicited, 1910 cases were excluded due to missing data, especially the starting time of the surgery to ensure accurate timing analysis, leaving a total of 7184 patients with operatively treated trochanteric femur fractures between January 5th, 2001, and April 19th, 2024. Variables and outcome measures The following parameters from the AQC database were considered for this study: patient’s age, sex, American Society of Anaesthesiologists (ASA) physical status classification system score, type of insurance (statutory or private), surgeon class (senior attending, junior attending, resident), length of surgery in minutes, the occurrence of any complication (yes or no), length of hospital stay in days, and discharge status (home, rehabilitation clinic, nursing home, old people’s home, death, and others). Complication comprised general (e.g. pneumonia, renal dysfunction), intraoperative (e.g. iatrogenic fractures, tissue damage) or postoperative (e.g. bleeding, infection, malreduction). No standardized frailty scoring system was applied and the fractures were not subclassified according to severity. We categorized the patients according to the preoperative interval (less or more than 24 h) to evaluate the influence of surgical delay. For further analysis, we stratified the patients into two additional groups based on the time of surgery start: ‘DAY,’ for surgeries starting between 7:00 a.m. and 6:59 p.m., and ‘NIGHT,’ for surgeries starting between 7:00 p.m. and 6:59 am. The occurrence of any complication during the hospitalization was the primary outcome, whereas in-hospital mortality was the secondary outcome. Statistical analysis The data was downloaded from the AQC database using the AdjumedAnalyze software (Adjumed Services AG, Zurich, Switzerland). The statistical analysis was executed in SPSS version 29.0.2.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). The chi-square test was employed for analysis of the categorical data, presented as absolute numbers of patients and their corresponding percentages. An unpaired t-test was performed to compare the numerical data, presented as means ± standard deviation (SD). A p -value of < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance. We utilized backward stepwise binary logistic regression as a statistical tool to explore and identify independent risk factors associated with the likelihood of any complication and death. ASA V and ASA I were excluded as predictors for mortality, since they were always associated (or not at all) with death. Results Study population A total of 7184 patients were included in the study. The mean age was 82 ± 11 years, the patients had predominantly a female sex (73%). An ASA score of II or III was recorded in 90% of patients, with 45% having ASA II and 45% ASA III, followed by ASA I with 6.3% and ASA IV with 2.9%. Statutory insurance covered 74% of the patients, and 42% of the surgeries were done by junior consultants, 30% by senior consultants, and 28% by residents. The length of surgery was 68 ± 39 min. The patients stayed 10 ± 6 days. After the hospital stay, 26% went home, 29% were discharged to a rehabilitation clinic, 15% to an old people’s home, and 19% to a nursing home (Table ). Preoperative delay of > 24 h Nine hundred and fifty patients (13%) received surgery after more than 24 h of hospitalization. These patients had similar age and sex as the group with a delay of less than 24 h, however, they had a significantly higher ASA score and a marginally greater coverage under statutory insurance. In the group with preoperative delay over 24 h, we observed a statistically significant difference in the length of surgery (70 ± 53 vs. 67 ± 37 min), occurrence of any complication (22% vs. 16%), and length of hospitalization (12 ± 7 vs. 10 ± 6 days). Also, patients were more often discharged to a nursing home (21% vs. 18%) or deceased (5.4% vs. 3.1%) and less often discharged home (24% vs. 26%) or to a rehabilitation clinic (28% vs. 30%) (Table ). Complications The overall complication rate was 17%. Surgery delayed beyond 24 h was associated with a 37.5% increase in the complication rate (22% vs. 16%). Binary logistic regression analysis identified delayed surgery > 24 h, an increased ASA score, male sex, higher age and longer surgery duration as significant risk factors for the occurrence of complications. (Table ) Hence, delayed surgery after 24 h was confirmed as an independent risk factor, indicating a 38% increased risk for the occurrence of any complication. Mortality The overall in-hospital

home (24% vs. 26%) or to a rehabilitation clinic (28% vs. 30%) (Table ). Complications The overall complication rate was 17%. Surgery delayed beyond 24 h was associated with a 37.5% increase in the complication rate (22% vs. 16%). Binary logistic regression analysis identified delayed surgery > 24 h, an increased ASA score, male sex, higher age and longer surgery duration as significant risk factors for the occurrence of complications. (Table ) Hence, delayed surgery after 24 h was confirmed as an independent risk factor, indicating a 38% increased risk for the occurrence of any complication. Mortality The overall in-hospital mortality was 3.4%. Delayed surgery was significantly associated with a 74% increase in the mortality rate (5.4% vs. 3.1%), but not a significant predictor for mortality in regression analysis. Binary logistic regression identified complications and advancing age as significant risk factors for mortality (Table ). Daytime versus nighttime surgery Among 2406 patients, the exact starting time of the surgery was available. The complication rate was similar between the daytime and nighttime groups ( p = 0.263), and mortality rates were also not statistically different ( p = 0.15). Including this dichotomous parameter in the logistic regression, the timing of surgery was not retained in the final regression model (Table ). Discussion Key findings Our study contributes additional evidence to the ongoing debate, whether delayed surgery > 24 h or nighttime surgery starting between 7:00 p.m. and 6:59 am increases the in-hospital complication and mortality rate. In this nationwide retrospective cohort study (evidence level III), we analysed 7184 patients with trochanteric femur fractures treated with CRIF during an almost 24-year period. In our study, patients receiving early surgery within 24 h of admission showed a better in-hospital outcome. Patients undergoing delayed surgery had an increased complication rate (22% vs. 17%). Preoperative delay was found to be an independent risk factor for the occurrence of complications, alongside with an increased ASA score, male sex, higher age, and longer surgery duration. Delayed surgery was significantly associated with mortality (5.4% vs. 3.1%), but not a significant predictor for mortality in the regression analysis. Independent risk factors for mortality were higher ASA scores, the occurrence of any complication, male sex, and advancing age. Nighttime surgery was not associated with a higher complication or mortality rate, nor was it a significant risk factor in multivariate analysis. While the timing of hip fracture surgery has been studied extensively, fracture-type-specific analyses remain rare. Implications Our findings highlight the critical role of early surgery within 24 h of admission in reducing in-house complications, mortality and hospital stay, particularly for trochanteric femur fractures. Preoperative delay emerged as the most modifiable predictor of adverse outcomes. Surgical delay did not predict mortality independently, but the occurrence of any complication. Concerns about night-time surgery should not justify delays. Instead, strategic prioritization can optimize resource allocation without compromising patient safety. Achieving timely intervention requires addressing systemic delays—especially staffing and surgical capacity—through hospital-level improvements and policy support. Multidisciplinary coordination, designated trauma rooms, and orthogeriatric care have proven effective in streamlining processes and improving outcomes. Fracture-specific guidance for trochanteric fractures could enhance current hip fracture protocols. While implementing a < 24-hour surgery target poses challenges, doing so benefits both patients and healthcare systems. Known evidence Demographics and baseline-outcome The typical patient in our study was an elderly woman with chronic comorbidities, reflecting a 3:1 female-to-male ratio consistent with existing literature [ , , , – ]. Our in-hospital mortality rate for trochanteric femur fractures was 3.4%, slightly above the 2.6% national average for all hip fractures in Switzerland but well within the international range of 1.9-7.0.0% for trochanteric fractures [ , , , , – ]. Reported in-house complication rates globally vary between 12 and 46% [ , , – , ]. Early surgery benefits for patients with hip fractures generally Multiple studies support early surgery (within 24 h) for patients with hip fractures, showing reduced 30-day and one-year mortality, especially in elderly patients without reversible contraindications. Welford et al.’s 2021 meta-analysis of 46 studies confirmed these findings (RR 0.86), even when comparing to a 24–36 h window [ ]. Earlier meta-analyses reported significantly fewer complications with surgery within 24 h, yet significant mortality benefits appearing only at one-year postoperatively [ , ]. Patients with comorbidities seem to benefit most of early surgery [ , ]. The Hip Fracture Accelerated Surgical Treatment and Care Track (HIP ATTACK) RCT found no additional advantage of surgery within 6 h versus 24 h for complications or mortality but did show quicker mobilization and shorter hospital stay [ ]. While medical optimization of patients with severe and reversible conditions is crucial and guidelines exist, surgical delays in comorbid patients were also shown to reflect capacity challenges [ , ]. Comparison with other studies Several studies support an association between surgical

only at one-year postoperatively [ , ]. Patients with comorbidities seem to benefit most of early surgery [ , ]. The Hip Fracture Accelerated Surgical Treatment and Care Track (HIP ATTACK) RCT found no additional advantage of surgery within 6 h versus 24 h for complications or mortality but did show quicker mobilization and shorter hospital stay [ ]. While medical optimization of patients with severe and reversible conditions is crucial and guidelines exist, surgical delays in comorbid patients were also shown to reflect capacity challenges [ , ]. Comparison with other studies Several studies support an association between surgical delays beyond 24 h and increased complication rates in trochanteric femur fractures. Daginnus et al. found this effect in Germany, but only for trochanteric – not femoral neck – fractures [ ]. Tanaka et al. observed similar results in Japan, albeit assessing a 48-hour-threshold for surgery [ ]. Vidan et al. reported the highest reported complication rate of 46% in acute hip surgery in Spain with a median delay of 72 h, largely due to operating room limitations [ ]. Pincus et al., in a Canadian study of 42,000 patients, identified 24 h as a key threshold for increased complications and 30-day mortality, though without fracture type differentiation [ ]. In a Swedish register analysis, Greve et al. linked delays over 24 h to worse outcomes, particularly in higher-risk patients [ASA III/IV and women] [ , ]. Other studies, such those by Delaveau [ ] and Schermann [ ], reinforce mortality benefits for surgery within 24 h, especially in the elderly. However, some studies like those by Tanner [ ], Orosz [ ], and Saul [ ] show mixed or minimal effects, likely due to small sample size, short delays, or heterogenous patient population. New contributions and strength of the study Despite extensive research upon acute hip fracture, many studies fail to differentiate between femoral neck and trochanteric fractures - two distinct entities which differ in pathophysiology, treatment, and outcomes [ , , , , ]. In trochanteric fractures, the lack of capsular confinement facilitates uncontained bleeding, soft tissue injury, inflammatory response, and are linked to higher complication and mortality rates, especially in older, frailer patients [ – ]. As the population ages, the incidence of trochanteric fractures is rising, particularly among men, making them increasingly relevant [ ]. Our study focuses specially on trochanteric fractures, confirming the association between surgical delay beyond 24 h and worse in-hospital outcome, while nighttime surgery was not found to be a risk factor. Closed reduction and intramedullary nailing, the standard treatment, is minimally invasive, resource-efficient, and manageable even by junior surgeons [ , ]. Avoiding night surgery due to staffing or logistical concerns contributes unnecessarily to surgical delay [ , , , , , , ]. While perceptions of nighttime risk persist, evidence from our study and others does not support increased harm in timely off-hour hip operations [ – ]. The large, multi-center cohort of over 7,000 patients strengthens the generalizability of our findings and underscores the need for fracture-specific guidelines - particularly as demographic shifts point to a growing burden of trochanteric fractures in aging populations [ ]. Limitations This study is limited trochanteric fractures treated with closed reduction and internal fixation; thus, findings cannot be generalized to complex cases or other procedures. Its retrospective design restricts causal inference, and stratifying solely by time to surgery may overlook necessary delay for medical optimization. Furthermore, procedural developments regarding surgical technique or management might have occurred over the 24 years observed. Registry-based analysis lacks detailed patient-level data, raising the risk of unmeasured confounding (e.g. reason for delay, hospital specific protocols, preoperative management). The AQC registry does not assess subdivisions of fracture or fixation type, neither orthogeriatric treatment, denying further analysis. No adjustments or propensity matching were performed. Generalizability is limited to healthcare systems with similar structures, and outcomes were restricted to the in-hospital period. Conclusion Minimizing surgical delays in trochanteric fractures is crucial, as unwarranted postponement increases the risk for adverse outcomes (complications, mortality) and costs without proven benefit. Night-time surgery was not associated with higher perioperative risk. While short delays for medical optimization may be justified, organizational improvements and orthogeriatric co-management are essential to ensure timely, safe surgery. With the rising incidence of fragility fractures, focused research and early multidisciplinary care remains key to improving outcomes and healthcare efficiency.

documents.title: ASA Practice Guidelines for Moderate Procedural Sedation and Analgesia

chunks.content: Introduction Background {6a} Gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy is a widely applied procedure for screening and treating upper GI diseases, particularly upper GI tumors. However, undergoing endoscopy without anesthesia may cause discomfort, nausea, vomiting, and even asphyxia [ ]. With advancements in anesthetic techniques, sedation has been increasingly used for GI endoscopy. Given the current situation, the number of sedated GI endoscopy procedures in China is expected to increase to 30 million in 2030. Patient safety during sedation for GI endoscopy is particularly important. Despite the application of oxygen supplementation using nasal cannulas, hypoxia continues to be one of the most common complications. Its incidence has been reported to range between 1.8% and 69% [ – ]. Insufficient ventilation caused by either hypoventilation or airway obstruction during deep sedation contributes to the occurrence of hypoxia. Long-term hypoxia can lead to coronary ischemia and permanent neurological damage, potentially leading to death [ ]. Relaxation of the upper airway muscles and increased susceptibility to airway collapse are unavoidable consequences of intravenous anesthesia. The main cause of hypoxia is upper airway obstruction caused by posterior displacement of the tongue [ , ]. Despite the advancements in methods for maintaining airway patency and preventing hypoxia during sedated endoscopy, such as jaw thrust as well as nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal airway insertions, notable limitations remain. Previous studies have shown that lifting the patient’s jaw in the lateral position is insufficient [ ] and labor-intensive for healthcare providers. Furthermore, nasopharyngeal airway insertion increases the risk for nasal bleeding, whereas oropharyngeal airways can interfere with endoscope insertion. To maintain airway patency and oxygenation, Professor Diansan Su invented the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway, which was comprehensively introduced in our previous letter [ ]. The advantages of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway include enhanced oxygenation, capnography, and endoscope navigation; reduced airway obstruction, particularly in patients with obesity; and provision of supraglottic jet ventilation. Our preliminary validation revealed that the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway can significantly reduce the incidence of hypoxia. Nevertheless, suboptimal sedation may lead to nausea and increased oral secretions during the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway implantation process, thereby affecting endoscopic procedures and even increasing the risk of airway accidents. Therefore, the device requires a relatively proper depth of sedation. On top of that,it remains to be validated by large-scale multicenter clinical studies. Thus, this study aims to evaluate the clinical efficiency of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway in sedated esophagogastroduodenoscopy. We hypothesize that the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway can reduce the incidence of hypoxia in patients undergoing endoscopy. Objectives {7} This study aims to determine whether the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway can reduce the incidence of hypoxia in patients undergoing GI endoscopy under propofol sedation. Primary objective Our primary objective is to determine the incidence of hypoxia (75% ≤ SpO 2 < 90% for < 60 s). Secondary objective Our secondary objective is to determine the incidence rate of subclinical hypoxia (90% ≤ SpO 2 < 95%); severe hypoxia (SpO 2 < 75% or 75% ≤ SpO 2 < 90% for ≥ 60 s); and other adverse events (AEs), which are tools proposed by the International Sedation Task Force established by the World Society of Intravenous Anesthesia. Hyphothesis {7} We hypothesize that the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway will reduce hypoxia incidence for patients undergoing GI endoscopy with sedation. Our aim is to provide credible evidence regarding the enhancement of patient safety during GI endoscopy procedures. Trial design {8} This multicenter, randomized, open-label, two-arm parallel-group interventional superiority clinical trial aims to assess the effects of the intervention. The patients will be randomly divided into two groups in a 1:1 ratio. For each selected patient, researchers will determine their grouping through a central randomization system, but patients will not be informed of their grouping. This trial will be conducted in accordance with the Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials (SPIRIT). The trial was registered in ClinicalTrials.gov (No. NCT06081647 ) on October 15, 2023. Methods Study setting {9} This study will enroll 1200 participants from the 10 aforementioned hospitals will be conducted in 10 tertiary university hospitals in China: Renji Hospital, The First Affiliated Hospital Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Xinhua Hospital (affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine); Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center, Tongji Hospital (affiliated with Shanghai Tongji University School of Medicine); The First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University, Shandong Provincial Qianfoshan Hospital (affiliated with Shandong First Medical University); The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University; The First Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University; and Tianjin Medical University General Hospital. Our clinical trial has been approved and supported by the ethics committee of the Renji Hospital Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine (LY2023-159-B). Eligibility criteria {10} Table summarizes the inclusion and exclusion criteria. All participating centers are high-volume, tertiary university hospitals in China with dedicated gastrointestinal

Our clinical trial has been approved and supported by the ethics committee of the Renji Hospital Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine (LY2023-159-B). Eligibility criteria {10} Table summarizes the inclusion and exclusion criteria. All participating centers are high-volume, tertiary university hospitals in China with dedicated gastrointestinal endoscopy units. To be eligible for participation, each center must meet the following criteria:(1) Perform a minimum of 5000 sedated GI endoscopy procedures annually. (2) Have a standardized sedation protocol for GI endoscopy led by qualified anesthesiologists. (3) Possess the necessary monitoring equipment, including capnography, pulse oximetry, non-invasive blood pressure, and electrocardiogram, in all procedure rooms. (4) Obtain approval from their respective local Institutional Review Board or Ethics Committee prior to initiating patient enrollment. (5) Designate a principal investigator at their site who is responsible for ensuring protocol adherence, staff training, and data quality. All procedural sedation and airway management will be performed by qualified healthcare professionals to ensure patient safety and protocol consistency. All sedating clinicians must be board-certified anesthesiologists with at least 1 year of independent practice experience in procedural sedation. They must complete a standardized training module on the study protocol (by offline or online conferences held through the main center), with a specific focus on the use of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway, including its insertion technique, confirmation of proper placement, and troubleshooting common issues. Competency will be assessed and documented prior to their participation in the trial. Who will take informed consent? {26a} Trained anesthesiologists at each participating center will approach potential participants during their arrival at the endoscopy unit, prior to the scheduled procedure. The consent discussion will take place in a private and quiet setting, such as a consultation room or a designated pre-operative area, to ensure confidentiality and minimize distractions. They will thoroughly explain the trial to potential participants, including a step-by-step explanation of the trial’s purpose, procedures, potential risks and benefits, and the rights of participants using plain language, and provide them with an informed consent form. Participants can decide whether to participate in the trial after careful consideration. Subsequently, participants or their representatives or guardians may sign the informed consent form and withdraw from the trial at any time. If a participant lacks the capacity to provide informed consent due to cognitive impairment or other reasons, their legally authorized representative or guardian will be consulted. This approach aligns with our inclusion criteria, which permit the enrollment of participants who are able to provide informed consent or have a legal representative who can do so on their behalf. Thereafter, the patients’ baseline data will be collected, followed by random patient allocation using a centralized randomization system. If participants experience any health issues during the trial, they can contact our team. Subject recruitment and agreement acquisition from members of the research team will be carried out in accordance with Good clinical practice (GCP) guidelines for drug clinical trials. Investigators will immediately report to the clinical trial leader at the research institution and contact Professor Diansan Su if any adverse events occur during the trial, whether or not related to the study procedures. Additional consent provisions for the collection and use of participant data and biological specimens {26b} Not applicable. No subject data or biological samples will be collected or utilized in this study. Patient and public involvement Patients and the public will not be directly involved in the formulation of the research question, development of the study design, or recruitment and implementation phases. Interventions Explanation for the selection of comparators {6b} The control group (Arm 1) will receive a conventional nasal cannula with capnography monitoring, which represents the current standard of care for oxygenation and ventilation monitoring during sedated gastrointestinal endoscopy in most clinical settings according to the guidelines. This comparator was selected for several scientific reasons. Firstly, the nasal cannula is widely used in clinical practice for oxygen delivery during procedural sedation and allows for direct comparison with the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway. By using the conventional nasal cannula as the comparator, we can objectively evaluate whether the COMBO device provides superior efficacy in preventing hypoxia without introducing confounding factors from unproven or non-standard devices. Secondly, hypoxia remains a common adverse event despite the use of nasal cannulas, highlighting a persistent clinical need. Comparing the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway against this established method will help determine whether it offers meaningful improvement in airway management. Intervention description {11a} Arms 1 and 2 will constitute the interventions in this trial.Control Group (Arm 1) will receive a standard endoscopy bite block to prevent biting the endoscope, along with a nasal cannula equipped with a CO 2 sampling port. Oxygen will be supplied at a flow rate of 3–4 L/min via the nasal cannula, with continuous monitoring of inhaled and exhaled CO 2 . Intervention Group (Arm 2) will receive the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway, an integrated device that combines the functions of a bite block, oxygen supply, and CO 2 sampling. The COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway provides an extra-oral oxygen delivery channel in addition to the nasal route, achieving dual-channel ventilation. Oxygen will be supplied at a total flow rate of 3–4 L/min, delivered through the nasal part of the device, consistent with the control group to ensure comparability. Sedation protocol In both groups, the following standardized sedation protocol will be applied: Administered for 1 min before the initiation of sedation. Then, Sufentanil 7 µg will be administered intravenously at the start of preoxygenation. After approximately 1 min of oxygen administration, propofol sedation will be initiated with an intravenous bolus of 1.5 mg/kg. Once a Ramsay Sedation Score of 5 or higher is achieved, the endoscopist will insert the endoscope and commence the procedure. Additional propofol boluses of 0.2–0.5 mg/kg will be intermittently administered as needed to maintain a Ramsay Sedation Score ≥ 5 throughout the examination. Timing The assigned intervention device (standard nasal cannula and bite block for Arm 1, or the bite block of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway for Arm 2) will be placed and oxygen flow initiated immediately at the start of the preoxygenation period, which begins 1 min before the administration of propofol. The airway part of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway will be immediately inserted after the patient’s Ramsay Sedation score reaches 5 or above. Criteria for discontinuing or modifying the allocated interventions {11b} If participants request to withdraw from the trial, the allocated intervention will be discontinued. A clinical rescue protocol will be immediately initiated step by step if a participant meets any of the following criteria, indicating a failure of the assigned intervention to maintain adequate oxygenation: Increase the oxygen flow rate to 6–8 L/min via the existing device ( for SpO₂ < 95% and/or PetCO 2 decreases by half or disappears, and/or chest wall undulations disappear ). Perform chin-lift or jaw-thrust maneuver ( for failure of STEP 1 ). Immediately withdraw the gastroscope and initiate bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation with 100% oxygen (for failure of STEP 2 ). proceed to advanced airway management (e.g., insertion of a laryngeal mask airway or endotracheal intubation) for mechanical ventilation ( for failure of STEP 3 or severe hypoxia- SpO₂ < 90% over 60 s ). We will strictly adhere to this protocol and record the last rescue method. Strategies to improve adherence to interventions {11c} Prior to trial initiation, all anesthesiologists involved in the study at each participating center will receive uniform training on the standard operating procedures for both the conventional nasal cannula (Arm 1) and the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway (Arm 2). This will ensure consistent application of the interventions across all sites. Key steps of the intervention, including the placement of the device and the initiation of oxygen flow, will be documented in the Case Report Form (CRF) for each participant. Every coordinating center will periodically review the CRFs to verify that the allocated intervention was correctly administered as per the protocol. Any deviations will be identified and addressed promptly. Relevant concomitant care permitted or prohibited during the trial {11d} All routine diagnostic and therapeutic procedures essential for the gastrointestinal endoscopy itself are permitted. Additionally, the use of standard medications to manage anticipated adverse events (AEs) per institutional practice is allowed and must be documented, such as administration of vasoactive drugs (e.g., ephedrine, atropine) for hemodynamic instability; use of additional airway maneuvers (e.g., jaw thrust) or reversal agents (e.g., flumazenil, naloxone) for respiratory depression; administration of antiemetics for nausea and vomiting. As to the alternative or additional airway devices (e.g., other types of oropharyngeal airways, nasopharyngeal airways, laryngeal mask airways) is prohibited, unless required as a rescue intervention for severe hypoxia or airway obstruction as defined in the trial procedures (see section Trial procedure {13}). Participant timeline{13} The schedule of enrollment, interventions, and assessments is summarized in Fig. (SPIRIT Figure). After providing written informed consent, eligible participants will be randomly assigned to one of the two groups. All study procedures will be completed during a single visit to the gastrointestinal endoscopy suite. We will select patients according to the inclusion and exclusion criteria for sedated upper GI endoscopy and include only those who have provided informed consent. In the GI endoscopy room, an anesthesiologist trained in the use of both the conventional nasal cannula and the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway will administer the sedative. Preoxygenation will be administered for 1 min before the initiation of sedation. Arm 1 will receive 3–4 L/min of oxygen via a conventional nasal cannula, whereas Arm 2 will receive oxygen at the same dose via the oxygen supply tube of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway (nasal part). A predetermined dose of sufentanil (7 µg) will be intravenously administered at the start of preoxygenation, according to Renji Hospital’s standard endoscopic anesthesia protocol. After approximately 1 min of oxygen administration, propofol sedation (1.5 mg/kg) will be administered intravenously. After the initiation of sedation, the anesthesiologist will closely monitor the patient and continuously assess the sedation depth using the Ramsay Sedation Scale. Once the Ramsay Sedation Score reaches 5 or higher, the endoscopist will insert the endoscope and commence the procedure. Propofol (0.2–0.5 mg/kg) will be intermittently administered until the examination is completed to maintain intra-procedural sedation. Objectives {12} This study aims to determine whether the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway can reduce the incidence of hypoxia and improve safety in patients undergoing GI endoscopy under propofol sedation. Sample size {14} According to the preliminary trial results and related literature, this study will use the PASS 15.0 software (two independent proportions, Fisher’s exact test) to estimate the sample size based on the difference in the incidence of hypoxia (75% ≤ SpO 2 < 90%, < 60 s) between Arms 1 and 2. Previous studies have reported that the incidence of hypoxia in patients in whom a conventional nasal cannula was used during painless gastroenterological endoscopy was approximately 8% [ ]. The parameters will be set as α = 0.05 and power = 0.8, with an expected reduction in hypoxia incidence from 8% to 4% and a dropout rate of 10%. The determined sample size is 1200 participants, randomly allocated in a ratio of 1:1, with 600 cases in Arm 1 and 600 in Arm 2. This multicenter study will enroll cases across centers on a competitive basis without a specific case number limit for each center. Recruitment {15} Achieving the target sample size of 1200 participants is anticipated to be feasible, given the vast volume of patients undergoing gastrointestinal endoscopy at the ten participating tertiary university hospitals across China. To ensure efficient and timely recruitment, we will implement the following active, multi-faceted strategy: A dedicated research coordinator at each site will proactively review the daily schedules of the gastrointestinal endoscopy centers to identify patients scheduled for procedures under propofol sedation. This allows for the early identification of a large pool of potential participants. Trained anesthesiologists or research staff will actively engage potential participants and their families, providing a clear and comprehensive explanation of the trial using standardized recruitment materials (e.g., brochures, posters). The communication will emphasize the following: (a) The potential benefit of receiving a novel device designed to reduce the risk of hypoxia, a common and concerning complication. (b) The safety of the intervention, explaining that it is integrated into the standard of care and does not alter the primary diagnostic or therapeutic procedure. (c) The minimal risk and burden to participants, as the study primarily involves the use of a different airway device during their already planned endoscopy. The presence of dedicated research staff whose primary responsibility includes patient recruitment will ensure consistent and enthusiastic engagement, preventing reliance on busy clinical staff alone. The subject recruitment and acquisition of informed consent by the research team will comply with the GCP guidelines. Assignment of interventions: allocation Sequence generation {16a} We will implement a stratified block randomization method within a centralized randomization system. Patient-specific, sedation-related, and procedural risk factors contribute to hypoxia during sedated GI endoscopy. Patient-specific risk factors mainly include preexisting cardiopulmonary conditions, obesity, and older age. The incidence of hypoxia during such procedures may vary based on the patients’ underlying health status. However, based on our inclusion criteria, eligible participants are those classified as ASA I–II; participants with more severe conditions, particularly those classified as ASA III–IV and those with significant preexisting cardiopulmonary diseases, will be excluded. Given this assumption, we will perform center-based rather than age-based stratification. We will collect participants’ baseline data, including personal information, such as name and birth date. Each sequence length is fixed at four. Concealment mechanism {16b} Allocation concealment will be ensured through the use of a centralized, web-based randomization system. The randomization sequence, generated using the stratified block method described in section {16a}, will be implemented and maintained within this system. When a participant provides informed consent and is deemed eligible for the trial, the site investigator will log into the secure online system to enroll the participant. The system will not reveal the upcoming group assignment until after the participant’s details have been irrevocably registered and the allocation is finalized. This process ensures that the investigators involved in participant enrollment cannot foresee or influence the assignment of any individual to a particular study group, thus maintaining concealment. Implementation {16c} The allocation sequence, generated by the centralized randomization system, will be implemented as follows: Designated physicians at each study site will enroll eligible participants. After obtaining informed consent, these physicians will access the centralized randomization system, input the necessary baseline data, and the system will then assign the participant to either Arm 1 or Arm 2 based on the pre-generated sequence. This process ensures a clear separation between sequence generation and participant enrollment/assignment. Blinding {17} Given the nature of the interventions (standard nasal cannula vs. the novel COMBO airway device), it is not feasible to blind trial participants or care providers (anesthesiologists and endoscopists) to the group assignment. This is an open-label trial from their perspective. However, to minimize potential bias, the following key roles will be blinded wherever possible: Outcome assessors: The assessment of the primary and secondary outcomes is based on objective, electronically recorded data from patient monitors.These data are stored in the electronic data capture (EDC) system. This process minimizes the need for subjective interpretation by an assessor who is aware of the group allocation, thereby reducing detection bias. Data analysts: The statisticians and data analysts will perform the final analyses while remaining blinded to the group allocation. The two intervention groups will be labeled in the data set with non-identifiable codes (e.g., “Arm 1”and “Arm 2”) until the final statistical model is locked and the analysis is complete. This ensures the objectivity of the analytical process and reduces interpretation bias. Plans to promote participant retention and complete follow‑up {18b} Given that this is a single-session trial, strategies for participant retention are primarily focused on ensuring completion of the study procedure after randomization. Strategies to prevent dropouts before the procedure The study procedure is fully integrated into the standard clinical pathway for sedated GI endoscopy. This minimizes the additional burden on participants, reducing a key incentive for withdrawal. Upon providing informed consent and being randomized, participants will proceed directly to the examine room. The time between randomization and the initiation of sedation is designed to be as short as possible, limiting opportunities for reconsideration or dropout. Also, the clinical team will reinforce the importance of completing the procedure for both clinical care and study integrity and will address any last-minute concerns the participant may have. Data collection from participants who deviate from the protocol or withdraw Intention-to-treat principle: he primary analysis will follow the intention-to-treat principle. All randomized participants will be included in the Full Analysis Set (FAS) and analyzed in the group to which they were originally assigned, regardless of protocol deviations or withdrawal. Data collection for protocol deviators For any participant who is randomized but subsequently deviates from the protocol (e.g., receives an inconsistent sedative dose, requires a prohibited rescue airway device, or withdraws consent after the procedure has started but before data collection is complete), we will collect and retain all available data up to the point of deviation or withdrawal. This includes the following: all baseline data (demographics, ASA, BMI, STOP-Bang score, etc.); any intra-procedure data that was recorded prior to the deviation (e.g., initial SpO₂, occurrence of hypoxia or other AEs); the reason for and nature of the protocol deviation or withdrawal. Statistical methods Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a} Data selection for statistical analysis Full analysis set (FAS): Following the intention-to-treat (ITT) approach, the FAS will include each participant who is randomized into the study and will receive the assigned treatment. The FAS will serve as the primary analysis set for all efficacy evaluations. Per-protocol set (PPS): The PPS will consist of FAS participants without major protocol deviations that could influence the assessment of primary outcomes. Such deviations may involve inconsistent sufentanil doses during the induction phase or a lack of primary outcome data. Efficacy evaluations will be conducted using the FAS and PPS datasets. Safety analysis set (SAS): The SAS will consist of all participants who will undergo the study treatment. Safety data analysis will be conducted exclusively on this group. Statistical methodology The statistical analysis plan will be developed before the trial concludes and finalized prior to database lock. It will include descriptive statistics and analytical methods. All statistical tests will be two-tailed and conducted using SPSS 23 (IBM, Armonk, NY). Furthermore, patient information will be expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Descriptive statistics for quantitative indicators will include the mean, standard deviation, median, minimum, and maximum values. Categorical variables will be expressed as numbers and percentages. The chi-squared tests will be employed to compare the incidence rates of hypoxia and AEs across the groups. Primary and secondary endpoints: These endpoints will be expressed as frequencies (incidence rates). Since the stratified block randomization by center ensures balance between groups within each center, the primary analysis for categorical outcomes will be performed using the Chi-squared tests without adjustment for center, as the randomization effectively controls for potential center effects. Moreover, we will also apply Fisher’s exact test where appropriate. A P -value < 0.05 will be considered statistically significant, with a 95% confidence interval. Postoperative adverse reactions (delirium, nasal congestion, nausea, and vomiting): These will be described using the number and percentage of cases. The incidence rates of adverse events will be compared using the chi-squared tests or Fisher’s exact probability test. For continuous outcomes, such as total propofol dose and procedure duration, we will use Student’s t -test for normally distributed data or the Mann-Whitney U test for non-normally distributed data. Additional analyses {20b} The overall safety assessment will focus on AE frequency and classification. Safety-related variables from all participants in the SAS will be organized into tables and presented accordingly. Categorization of AEs will be performed using the standardized terminology developed by the International Working Party on Sedation under the World Intravenous Anesthesia Society. The proportion of participants who will experience at least one AE will be analyzed using appropriate statistical methods, such as the chi-squared test, chi-squared test with continuity correction, or Fisher’s exact test, depending on the data distribution. Interim analyzes {21b} No formal interim analysis for efficacy or futility is planned for this trial. However, the trial may be stopped prematurely based on the recommendation of the Ethics Committee on the following grounds: Safety concerns: if evidence emerges of clear and unacceptable harm to participants associated with the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway Protocol violations: if significant and persistent protocol deviations are identified that compromise the scientific integrity of the trial or participant safety External evidence: if new, definitive evidence from other studies emerges that renders the continuation of this trial unnecessary or unethical The Principal Investigator (PI), Professor Diansan Su, in consultation with the sponsoring institution, holds the ultimate authority to suspend or terminate the trial for safety reasons. This decision will be based on a thorough review of all available safety data and will be promptly communicated to the coordinating investigators, all study sites, the Ethics Committee, and the trial registry. Access will be granted for approved scientific research purposes following the signing of a data use agreement, which will include commitments to using the data only for the agreed purpose, securing the data appropriately, and not attempting to re-identify participants. The full protocol can also be provided upon request. Oversight and monitoring Composition of the coordinating center and trial steering committee {5d} Trial management group (TMG) The TMG comprises all members of the research team (see Supplementary Material for the full list). The TMG is responsible for the day-to-day management of the trial, including participant recruitment, data collection, protocol adherence, and communication among centers. Trial steering committee (TSC) The TSC is an independent oversight body and includes the following members: Professor Diansan Su (Chair), Dr. Yueying Zheng, Professor Jianbo Wu, and Professor Yonghao Yu. The TSC is responsible for overall trial supervision, reviewing major decisions, ensuring participant safety, and providing guidance on scientific and ethical issues. Executive committee The Executive Committee consists of the principal investigators and site coordinators from each participating center (see Supplementary Material for details). This committee is responsible for the local implementation of the trial, ensuring compliance with the protocol, and facilitating site-specific training and quality assurance. Statistical team The statistical analysis will be independently conducted by Dr. Wei Zhang’s team from the Department of Biostatistics, Fudan University. They are responsible for data management, statistical analysis plan development, and final analyses, as well as ensuring the integrity and validity of the trial results. Composition of the data monitoring committee, its role and reporting structure {21a} A formal, independent Data Monitoring Committee (DMC) will not be established for this trial because the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway is a device-based intervention designed to improve oxygenation and maintain airway patency. It does not involve a novel pharmaceutical agent with unknown systemic toxicity. Moreover, the device functions as an integrated bite block with additional oxygenation and monitoring capabilities, building upon standard of care components. Therefore, the anticipated risks are not greater than those associated with routine sedated gastrointestinal endoscopy.The trial employs continuous, real-time monitoring of vital signs (including SpO₂, ECG, and capnography) by a dedicated anesthesiologist throughout the procedure. Any adverse event, such as hypoxia, will be immediately detected and managed according to a pre-specified, standardized rescue protocol. This robust intraoperative safety mechanism reduces the need for a DMC to review unblinded data for emergent safety concerns. At last, hypoxia is a common, transient, and readily reversible event in the context of procedural sedation. It does not constitute a long-term or irreversible harm to participants. The risk profile of this outcome is well understood, and its management is routine in clinical practice. Adverse event reporting and harms {22} Though there has been no evidence that this study may cause any risk or discomfort to the participants, this trial still systematically records and evaluates all adverse events (AEs), defined as any untoward medical occurrence in a participant who has received the trial intervention. Special attention will be given to serious adverse events (SAEs), which are defined as any events that result in death, are life-threatening, require inpatient hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization, result in significant disability or congenital anomaly, or constitute other important medical events. All AEs

is routine in clinical practice. Adverse event reporting and harms {22} Though there has been no evidence that this study may cause any risk or discomfort to the participants, this trial still systematically records and evaluates all adverse events (AEs), defined as any untoward medical occurrence in a participant who has received the trial intervention. Special attention will be given to serious adverse events (SAEs), which are defined as any events that result in death, are life-threatening, require inpatient hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization, result in significant disability or congenital anomaly, or constitute other important medical events. All AEs will be assessed for both severity and causality. Severity will be graded as mild (easily tolerated), moderate (interferes with usual activity), or severe (incapacitating), while the relationship to the trial intervention will be categorized as “related” or “not related.” For reporting, all non-serious AEs will be documented in the source documents and case report forms for subsequent review by the Trial Management Group and Trial Steering Committee. Any SAE must be reported immediately. Upon awareness of an SAE, the site investigator is required to notify the sponsor (Professor Diansan Su) within 24 h, followed by a detailed written report to the sponsor and the Ethics Committee within the same timeframe. All SAEs will be actively followed until resolution. Frequency and plans for auditing trial conduct {23} A formal, independent audit of the trial conduct is not planned. This decision is based on the following considerations: the trial evaluates a non-pharmacological, device-based intervention with a well-established safety profile; it employs a robust, multi-layered internal monitoring system including continuous oversight, and all study procedures are conducted under the principles of Good Clinical Practice (GCP) with source data verification performed during routine monitoring. The existing oversight structure is deemed sufficient to ensure the scientific integrity of the trial and the protection of participants’ rights and safety. Plans for communicating important protocol amendments to relevant parties (e.g., trial participants and ethical committees) {25} This clinical trial will be conducted according to the approval granted by the ethics committee. Any issues or amendments to the protocol that arise during the trial course will be promptly communicated to the ethics committees, trial participants, trial registries, journals, and regulatory authorities. Protocol changes will only be implemented with prior approval from the ethics committee. Dissemination plans {31a} The participants, healthcare professionals, public, and other relevant groups will communicate the results of this trial in the form of articles. Trial status Recruitment for the trial was scheduled to start on November 27, 2023, and is expected to conclude on December 1, 2025. Patient enrollment will take place at 12 designated hospitals. Discussion This study will be the first randomized controlled trial to systematically evaluate the impact of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway on the reduction of hypoxia incidence in patients undergoing sedated GI endoscopy. Sedation for GI endoscopy has been increasingly applied worldwide. Ensuring patient safety during sedation for GI endoscopy is crucial. Hypoxia continues to be the most significant concern among patients undergoing GI endoscopy under propofol sedation [ , ]. Severe or persistent hypoxia often requires airway interventions, which may increase the risk for sedation-related AEs, such as hypotension, respiratory depression, and delayed recovery [ ]. Thus, maintaining oxygenation is crucial during sedated GI endoscopy. Several studies have investigated various methods to reduce the incidence of hypoxia during sedated GI endoscopy, including capnography [ ], supplemental oxygen [ ], different sedative agents [ ], and other ventilation techniques [ ]. However, none of them can effectively address the problem of airway patency. The COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway is a novel device that combines real-time monitoring of ventilation status through capnography and a direct mechanical intervention to maintain airway patency, which may be an effective adjunct to existing monitoring strategies, further enhancing patient safety during endoscopy procedures. Our study will be the first multicenter, randomized clinical trial to systematically evaluate the impact of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway on hypoxia during GI endoscopy under propofol sedation. Our study is expected to provide high-quality evidence and improve the safety of sedated GI endoscopy. Nevertheless, our study has several limitations. First, it is an open-label clinical study, which may introduce potential bias. Second, it is not international; it only includes tertiary general hospitals in China, where sedative drugs or methods may differ across different institutions and countries. Third, we include only patients with normal body weight (18.5 < BMI < 30); thus, the effectiveness of airway management in patients who are overweight was not determined. We have planned a targeted study focusing on overweight patients in our future research. Our study has important clinical implications for managing patients undergoing GI endoscopy under propofol sedation. The incorporation of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway into routine practice could markedly reduce the risk
